beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Scientific Reproducibility Two: Version Control. Learn to use Git so that every result you produce, on a laptop or on a cluster, can be tied to the exact code that made it.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. Version control is not a backup folder. It is a timeline of snapshots you can search, compare and rewind, and each snapshot can be tied to the result it produced.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. Repository: the project folder plus its history. Commit: a saved snapshot of your files. Branch: a movable name for one line of commits. Tag: a fixed name for one commit. The git ignore file: a list of what Git skips. And a Slurm job: your request for a compute node.

beats.narration_text: Six months after you submit a paper, a reviewer asks: what threshold did you use for low-count filtering? Without version control you open a folder like this, and you guess from the file names. Which script made which table?

beats.narration_text: Version control replaces that folder with one script and a timeline. Every change carries a date, an author and a message. You can mark the exact code behind a figure, give each experiment its own branch, and undo a bad change.

beats.narration_text: The program is called Git, and its idea is simple. It stores snapshots, not edits. A commit is a full picture of your files at one moment, linked to the commit before it.

beats.narration_text: Your files live in three places. The working tree is what you see and edit. The staging area is the list of changes going into the next snapshot, and git add puts a change there. The repository holds the saved snapshots, and git commit saves them.

beats.narration_text: Four moments where this saves you. A reviewer asks if you tried another value: open the branch where you did. A postdoc leaves: clone the repository and read the README. A cluster setting changed: diff against the last commit. Publishing the code with the paper: tag a release on GitHub.

beats.narration_text: The example is a small R N A sequencing project: a table of read counts, one row per gene, three control columns and three treated. One script drops low-count genes, works out a fold change, and writes a summary. Any analysis follows the same Git workflow.

beats.narration_text: This is the script we will track. Strict mode, an input, an output, and a parameters block at the top, where the one tunable value lives: min count, ten. Genes with a low mean count are skipped. The rest are called up, down, or not significant by fold change.

props.title: scripts/filter_and_summarise.sh  ·  from the source
lines: set -euo pipefail   # exit on error, unset var, pipe failure
# ── PARAMETERS ── change these, then commit before re-running
MIN_COUNT=10        # filter: remove genes with mean count below this

beats.narration_text: Start tracking before the first run, not after. Git init makes a hidden dot git folder: Git's database, one per project. A caution: depending on your settings, the first branch may be called master, as it was here, and the later steps say main. So rename it first.

beats.narration_text: Track the code that makes results, not the results themselves. Big raw data lives in project storage, outside the repository, and passwords or tokens never go in at all. Whatever Git should skip goes in a file named dot git ignore.

beats.narration_text: Here is the source's version of that file. It ignores the whole results folder, then lists two files to let back in: the summary table and the run log.

show.event: lines print as they are spoken

props.title: .gitignore  ·  from the source
lines: # ── Raw data (large — store in institutional repository)
!results/summary.tsv     # the table itself is small enough to track
!results/run.log         # the run log is the audit trail

beats.motion_claim: The text, exactly as written or as recorded, prints line by line as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: Run that in real Git and it fails. Git never looks inside an ignored folder, so it never reads the two allow lines. The add is refused, and check-ignore names line two of the file as the reason.

show.event: lines print as they are spoken

props.title: git refuses  ·  recorded on a Mac
lines: The following paths are ignored by one of your .gitignore files:
hint: Use -f if you really want to add them.

beats.motion_claim: The text, exactly as written or as recorded, prints line by line as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: The fix is one character. Ignore the folder's contents, with slash star, not the folder. Now the folder itself is not ignored, so the two allow lines work, and both files stage.

show.event: lines print as they are spoken

props.title: the fix  ·  recorded on a Mac
lines: # in .gitignore, ours: ignore the contents, not the folder

beats.motion_claim: The text, exactly as written or as recorded, prints line by line as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: A second trap, in the same file. The source puts a comment after the pattern, on the same line. Git does not read that as a comment: the text becomes part of the pattern, which then matches nothing. So the add is still refused. Give every comment a line of its own.

# comments need a line of their own

beats.narration_text: Write the README before the first commit. List the requirements, the exact commands to reproduce the result, including the tag to check out, and the parameters. It is a contract with anyone who clones the repository, and that includes you in a year.

| `MIN_COUNT` | 10 | Minimum mean count to keep a gene |

beats.narration_text: The habit for every result: change a value, run the script, look at the output, then commit the code and the result together. Repeat. Before a paper goes out, tag the commit. That ties each result to the code and the parameters behind it.

beats.narration_text: Three commands you will use dozens of times a day. Status shows what changed. Add chooses what goes into the next snapshot: that is the staging area. Commit saves it. The source stages everything with a dot; in a folder holding data, tokens or logs, name the files instead.

beats.narration_text: Now run it. The log names the commit, and the counts are there: two hundred genes, a hundred ninety-nine kept. But look at the date error and the empty brackets. Dash dash i s o is a G N U option, so it fails on a Mac. It should work on Linux, but we did not run this on a cluster. On a Mac, use date dash u with a format.

beats.narration_text: Then commit the results together with the code that made them, and let the message say what the run was. The log inside this commit names the commit before it, so the result carries its own receipt. That only works because the fixed git ignore file lets the two files through.

beats.narration_text: Two habits make a history worth reading. One logical change per commit: if the message needs the word and, make two commits. And a consistent message style, a type, a scope and a short summary, so git log reads like a change log and grep finds things.

Bottom: six type chips (feat, fix, data, analysis, docs, config) in a row, then one full example in mono 'analysis(fig3): reproduce with corrected normalization'.

beats.narration_text: Before you commit anything, look at what you are about to commit. Change the threshold, and git diff shows it line by line: one line out, one line in. The source edits with sed, and that form fails on a Mac, which wants an empty backup suffix after dash i. We used the Mac form.

beats.narration_text: The log is your audit trail. Stat shows which files each commit touched. Grep finds every commit that mentions a word, so the reviewer's question now has an answer in two lines. Dash p shows every change to one file, and git blame says who wrote each line, and when.

beats.narration_text: A reviewer asks you to try a fold change cutoff of one point five instead of two. You do not know yet whether it goes in the paper. So never edit the working script for a speculative change. Make a branch: a parallel version that leaves main untouched.

beats.narration_text: A tag is a flag on one commit, and it does not move. Branch names slide forward with every new commit; a tag stays where you planted it. Before the paper goes out, tag the commit behind your figures, and check that tag out any time to get exactly that code.

beats.narration_text: The tag command, and the list that shows it with its message. Tags are not sent by a plain push. Pushing uploads your work to a server such as GitHub, which changes something outside your machine, so do it on purpose and with the repository owner's agreement. We did not push; this folder has no remote.

beats.narration_text: The reviewer's question: what did you get with the original threshold? Find the commit by its message, restore only that one file from it, run it, and read the answer: a hundred ninety-nine genes kept at ten, against one ninety-seven at twenty. Then put today's version back.

beats.narration_text: On a cluster, a Slurm job runs later, on another machine, from the files as they are then. So two rules. Commit before you submit, so every job traces to one commit. And print that commit's hash in the job log, so the result always points back to the code.

beats.narration_text: Questions people ask. Can Git hold large datasets? Not directly. Git L F S handles files up to about two gigabytes, and D V C layers on Git and keeps the data elsewhere; track a manifest in Git. Jupyter notebooks carry their outputs, which makes noisy diffs: strip them with nbstripout, or sync with Jupytext.

beats.narration_text: To fix the last commit before you push, use commit dash dash amend. To undo a commit that is already shared, use git revert, which adds a new commit that undoes it. And never run git reset dash dash hard on a branch other people use: it throws work away.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A commit is a saved snapshot, and a tag is a fixed name for one of them. Track the code that makes results, and write the ignore file so its allow lines really work. Run, look, then commit the code and the result together, one logical change at a time. A branch holds an experiment; merge it when it belongs, and tag what you submit. Any old result comes back from its commit, one file at a time. On a cluster, commit before you submit, print the hash in the job log, and guard against a dirty tree.
